Superfluity
soo-per-FLOO-i-tee
noun
From the Latin superfluus, overflowing — super, above, and fluere, to flow. That which flows over the top; excess, overplus, more than is needed or contained.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, in James’s instruction on receiving the word: “Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls” (Jas 1:21). The image is agricultural and surgical at once. Superfluity of naughtiness is the overflow of wickedness — evil so abundant that it runs over the sides — and the verb lay apart is the word for stripping off a garment. James is describing a man taking off filthy clothes before receiving something into himself. Then comes the striking word engrafted: the word of God is to be received as a graft is received into a stock, which requires a cut, an insertion, and a binding, and which results in the graft’s nature prevailing over the stock’s. Note the order James insists on. Stripping comes before receiving, and meekness is the manner of receiving — not because the stripping earns the word, but because a man cannot receive a graft while refusing the knife. And observe what the engrafted word is said to do: it is able to save your souls. James, so often accused of preaching mere morality, here makes the word of God the instrument of salvation and meekness the posture of the saved.

Webster 1828 Definition

Overflow or excess; more than enough. In Jas 1:21, the overflowing abundance of wickedness that must be stripped off before the word is received.

SUPERFLUITY, n. A greater quantity than is wanted; superabundance.

That which is beyond what is necessary or useful.

From the Latin superfluus, from super, above, and fluere, to flow.

Jas 1:21: superfluity of naughtiness, the overflow of wickedness.

Naughtiness in the older English is wickedness, not mere mischief.

Key Scripture

Jas 1:21 — "Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls."

Jas 1:22 — "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."

1Pe 2:1 — "Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings,"

1Pe 2:2 — "As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby :"

Modern Corruption

Naughtiness has softened into a word for childish mischief, so a verse about the overflow of wickedness now sounds like a caution against harmless naughty behaviour.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The distortion is the softening of naughtiness. In 1611 the word meant wickedness outright — a naughty person was a worthless and evil one, as when Jeremiah’s bad figs are called naughty figs, or Eliab accuses David of a naughty heart. Modern English has reduced it to the mild misbehaviour of children, so that superfluity of naughtiness now sounds almost playful. The result is that one of the sharpest commands in the epistles reads like a caution against being a bit cheeky. Restore the word and the sentence recovers its edge: strip off, as a filthy garment, the overflowing abundance of your wickedness.

Recover the plain sense: James is not describing a tidy-up but a stripping, and the reason is the graft. A word received as an engrafted thing is not information added to a man but a nature introduced into him, and grafting requires a wound. Peter uses the identical structure: laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings, as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word (1Pe 2:1–2). Put off, then take in. And James will not let the receiving stay theoretical, for the very next verse says be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. The graft that takes will bear its own fruit, and a graft that bears nothing was never joined.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin super + fluere, to flow over — excess; the overflow of wickedness stripped off before the word is engrafted.

expand to see more

Superfluity — Latin superfluus, overflowing.

Jas 1:21 is its only occurrence in the Authorized Version.

Naughtiness in older English means wickedness (Jer 24:2; 1Sa 17:28).

Lay apart renders a verb for stripping off a garment.

Engrafted implies a cut, an insertion, and a nature that prevails.

Usage

"Read naughtiness as wickedness, not childish mischief."

"The order is stripping, then receiving, then doing (Jas 1:21–22)."

"1Pe 2:1–2 uses the identical put-off-then-take-in structure."
